title: Why jazz must be defined; the Modern Jazz Quartet
summary: Rose argues critics never define jazz, so the word means nothing. He says the MJQ derives from European chamber music, not jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Now, concerning, I'd like to concentrate a little bit on one of those activities, which is not only of interest to you, but to me also, which is jazz. And this will cross some of the other things you do in your work in records, record engineering, and producing concerts. I'm very interested in your definition of jazz. Okay. And how you came to define it this way, and why you feel it's necessary to define it.

Oh, certainly. Actually, all cultural forms about which experts write usually, invariably, have a fundamental set of criteria which are necessary in order for people to be able to deal with them intelligently. Now, most important is this, and that is that when any critic or expert discusses any subject, be it an art idiom or otherwise, his first actual responsibility is to define the area of his discussion. He has to be able to know what it is that he is being an expert on. And it has been increasingly obvious over the years that jazz has been made an exception to this, in that the so-called critic or expert does not feel a responsibility to define the subject before he discusses it, which leads to the kinds of exercise in futility that make it possible for the use of the word itself, as it is commonly and currently used, to be a complete irrelevancy, since it has no meaning at all as it is used. It means whatever the speaker or writer chooses to say it is. Therefore, it makes it extremely confusing for people coming to the subject for the first time to be able to recognize and identify the music when they hear it. As a result, the word having become a catch-all for a large variety of musical styles, including and excluding genuine jazz, has been used so that the people who write about it or talk about it automatically feel it necessary to include all of that material of which they personally approve under the heading of jazz and exclude everything else and say, well, this is not jazz.
Might they be using it as a general descriptive term?

Well, I would hope that they would do that, except for the fact that as it is used, it is in fact not descriptive of anything. For instance, I would consider it to be the suggestion that Guy Lombardo is the leader of a jazz band to have very tenuous merit. Yeah, I think... Except for the fact that it, in fact, is and has been used by those people who consider anything other than concert music to be jazz, which represents a substantial group in our population. Likewise, the music of such groups as the badly misnamed but extremely competent group called the Modern Jazz Quartet.

This is a group which is made of extremely competent musicians, all of whom I know personally, and for whom I have the greatest respect as musicians, but who have literally no relation to jazz at all. There is no jazz derivation, and there is no, no, what I would call jazz intent. This kind of a group is a direct offspring of European chamber music, modern European chamber music, and owes its debts to Hindemith and Stravinsky and Bartok and Ravelle. And, uh...

Okay, but how do you fit in the fact that, for instance, they have, uh... Oh, uh... One of the players plays a bass, and there's a beat that's, uh... That's a rhythmic beat that is, uh... identified with jazz or with Afro-American...

Uh... I'm contending that that actually does not occur. Uh-huh. And that all of those elements which you are mentioning already do exist in these other composers. Uh-huh. Uh... Daviesi's Gollywag Cakewalk, for example, contains precisely those elements before the Modern Jazz Quartet
existed. In other words, there's nothing Afro-American about the Modern Jazz Quartet.
